headline: Marathon AM holds CME Group as a high-quality franchise trading at or below S&P average despite superior margins and structural growth drivers.
reasoning: CME Group is a Marathon portfolio holding trading at just over 20 times forward earnings, at or below S&P market average, despite margins above 60% and almost no capital requirements. The business benefits from network effects in liquidity pools that competitors cannot easily replicate, and from a dominant market share in rates futures that a new entrant (FMX) has failed to dent after two years. Revenues are geared to uncertainty itself, with record volumes of 36 million contracts per day in Q1 across all six asset classes. The exchange can semi-endogenously grow by listing new contracts — including GPU rental rate futures — with little incremental cost. Key risks are regulatory (lighter-touch regulation allowing Kalshi-type competitors) and pricing mix shift towards cheaper contracts, but Marathon believes these are priced in after a decade of index underperformance.
quote: CME now sits among the quality franchises left behind by a market occupied with the AI story, even while it builds the venues where the story will be hedged. CME trades at just over 20 times forward earnings. ICE is more below that, which is at or below the S&P market average. For businesses with margins above 60%, almost no capital requirements, and revenues geared to uncertainty itself.

headline: Marathon's 2021 thesis that fintech disruption of Visa and Mastercard would not materialise proved correct, and the same logic now applies to exchange competition fears.
reasoning: In 2021, market consensus held that new fintechs were about to displace Visa and Mastercard; Marathon wrote about this at the time and argued the disruption would not materialise. That view proved correct. Marathon draws a direct parallel to the current concern that FMX and other new entrants, backed by major banks and offering cheaper fees, will erode CME's interest rate franchise. Two years after FMX's launch, its share of rates futures remains in the low single digits and open interest has not migrated, consistent with the network-effects logic Marathon applied to payment networks.
quote: Both stocks have derated over the past year or so on essentially three worries, new competitors, a laissez-faire regulator letting in lighter weight rivals, and a sense that some of the growth might be speculative throth. The question for us is whether the market spotted the beginning of the end of the exchange model or whether this is a rerun of 2021 in payments when everyone was convinced that the new fintechs were about to displace Visa and MasterCard. We wrote about that at the time and the disruptions yet materialize.

headline: Regulatory risk from CFTC's lighter-touch approach to prediction markets and Kalshi is the most serious threat to the exchange moat, though Marathon's base case is containment to retail event contracts.
reasoning: Much of the derivatives exchange moat is conferred by regulation: running a clearinghouse requires designation, capital, default funds, and supervision as systemically important, which deters casual entrants. The CFTC has allowed Kalshi to offer event contracts under a much lighter regulatory wrapper, and Kalshi is now pushing into equity perpetuals. CME sued its own regulator in June over this issue. However, Kalshi faces 19 separate state and federal actions, the CFTC brought its first insider trading case involving event contracts in April, and in June proposed retightening the public interest test it had recently loosened. Marathon's base case is that the lighter regulatory wrapper survives only for small retail event contracts, not for systemically important markets.
quote: This is the risk I take most seriously, precisely because so much of the moat is conferred by regulation. So to run a clearinghouse, you need designation, capital, default funds, and tolerance for being supervised is systemically important, which deters the casual entrance. But what the regulatory body, the relevant one the CFTC has done is let Kalshi, the prediction market, offer sports and political event contracts, and lately Bitcoin Perpetuals, under a much lighter wrapper than a traditional designated contract market carries. Our base case is that a lighter wrapper survives for small retail event contracts, but not for markets that are systemically important.

headline: Marathon AM holds Intercontinental Exchange, citing dominant clearing moat, mortgage technology optionality, and valuation below S&P average.
reasoning: ICE is a Marathon portfolio holding trading below 20 times forward earnings, at or below the S&P market average, despite an exchange segment running at around 80% adjusted operating margin and group revenues growing 18% last quarter with adjusted earnings growing roughly twice that. ICE's clearing methodology runs across more than 1,000 energy contracts and allows clients to net correlated positions, posting materially less collateral — an effective price cut no entrant can match without the same breadth of product. ICE has also built a portfolio of mortgage technology businesses with dominant positions in origination and servicing software, which is near cyclical trough due to high rates but could recover. Like CME, ICE is expanding into compute contracts and data center infrastructure to capture AI volatility, benefiting from the AI boom without owning a single GPU.
quote: ICE tells a similar story. The exchange segment runs at around an 80% adjusted operating margin. Last quarter, group revenues grew 18%. Adjusted earnings grew about twice that. And ICE has announced its own compute contracts and is expanding its data center estate to sell low latency access. In fact, they stand to benefit from the same AI boom without owning a single GPU. And earn more, the less anyone can agree on what the compute is worth.

headline: Listed US derivatives exchanges benefit from liquidity network effects and semi-endogenous growth that make them structurally resistant to disruption, akin to payment networks in 2021.
reasoning: Derivatives exchanges like CME and ICE operate as toll collectors on volatility, earning fees from both sides of a trade regardless of direction, with margins above 60% and minimal capital requirements. Their competitive moats are rooted in liquidity pools and clearing breadth rather than fee schedules, making them analogous to payment networks — a comparison reinforced by the failed fintech disruption of Visa and Mastercard. Unlike most businesses, exchanges can manufacture their own end markets by listing new contracts on any new source of price volatility using the same clearinghouse infrastructure, at almost no incremental cost. Both stocks have derated over the past year on fears of new competitors, lighter-touch regulation, and speculative volume, but Marathon believes these risks are priced in.
quote: Fee schedule can be copied overnight, but a liquidity pool can't. And what an exchange sells isn't really execution, which is almost incidental. It's the assurance that the other side of the trade will be there at a fair price today and in five years when you want out. Every contract that stays put deepens that assurance. So a would-be disruptor faces similar issues that the FinTechs ran into with the payment networks, i.e. lack of distribution.

headline: AI compute is beginning to exhibit commodity-like price volatility, creating the conditions for a derivatives market in GPU rental rates — a new growth avenue for CME and ICE.
reasoning: Renting an Nvidia H100 GPU for a year cost about 40% more in March than in October the prior year — the kind of price behaviour that historically summons a futures curve into existence, as happened with oil in the 1970s and electricity in the 1990s. CME has listed GPU rental rate futures with index provider Silicon Data (subject to approval) and ICE has announced compute contracts while expanding its data center estate for low-latency access. The exchanges stand to benefit from the AI boom without owning a single GPU, and earn more the less anyone can agree on what compute is worth, making this an example of the semi-endogenous growth model applied to a new asset class.
quote: AI starting to behave like a commodity. Prices that swing, buyers who need certainty, producers who want to lock in returns on enormous fixed investments. So renting one of Nvidia's H100 chips for a year cost about 40% more in March than it did in October last year. And historically, that's exactly the sort of price behavior that summons a futures curve into existence. It happened with oil in the 70s and electricity in the 90s. They stand to benefit from the same AI boom without owning a single GPU. And earn more, the less anyone can agree on what the compute is worth.

headline: Marathon AM views Fuyao Glass as a high-conviction buy, trading at a decade-low 12x forward earnings with a 4.5% dividend yield, as the world's dominant auto glass maker benefits from a turning capital cycle.
reasoning: Fuyao Glass is the world's largest auto glass manufacturer, holding approximately 70% of the Chinese market and a 35% global share, up from 20% in 2015. The company benefits from a powerful capital cycle tailwind: Western competitors (NSG, Saint-Gobain, AGC) are cutting capacity due to shrinking domestic car production and high energy costs, while Fuyao is expanding capacity by over 30% in the last two years. EV adoption is structurally positive, as EVs use more glass and more functional glass, lifting glass value per vehicle at 9% per annum over the last five years. Fuyao spends 4-5% of revenue on R&D — more than twice its nearest rival AGC in absolute terms — driving continuous innovation. Returns on invested capital are approaching 30% and return on equity approximately 26%, and the company has paid over 60% of earnings as dividends consistently over the last decade. At 12x forward earnings with a 4.5% dividend yield, the valuation is at a decade low as investors focus on depressed Chinese auto sales, which Marathon believes is an excellent entry point.
quote: We believe the valuation is very attractive at the moment as investors are fixated by the depressed auto sales in China and have marked down Fuyao's shares to a decade-low multiple of 12 times forward earnings with a 4.5% dividend yield, giving us what we believe is an excellent entry point. We saw Fuyao's return on invested capital climbing towards 30% and return equity approaching 26%. This is very rare for an industrial business. And relative to most Chinese companies, Fuyao is generous to shareholders, as they have paid out over 60% of their earnings continuously over the last decade as dividends.

headline: Japan's NSG (Nippon Sheet Glass) was taken private by Apollo in early 2025, likely to sweat assets rather than expand auto glass capacity.
reasoning: NSG's auto glass revenue is about half of Fuyao's. It was taken private by Apollo in March of the current year. The private equity ownership model suggests the business will focus on sweating existing assets rather than investing in new capacity, which removes it as a meaningful competitive threat to Fuyao and further tightens the global supply picture.
quote: Japan's NSG, whose autoclass revenue is about half of Fuyao's, was taken private by Apollo earlier this year in March. And they seem to be more likely to sweat their assets than expanding them.

headline: Saint-Gobain is closing European auto glass plants and plans to shrink or sell underperforming industrial assets, reinforcing the positive capital cycle for Fuyao.
reasoning: Saint-Gobain closed its automotive glass plants in Germany and Spain in the second half of last year, citing high energy costs and low-cost competition from China. Its five-year strategic plan explicitly targets shrinking or selling underperforming industrial assets, with auto glass a likely candidate for disposal. This capacity exit from the West is a key structural tailwind for Fuyao's global market share gains.
quote: France, St. Gabon has closed their automotive glass plants in Germany and Spain in the second half of last year, citing energy costs and low cost competition. In the next five years strategic plan, they seek to shrink or sell underperforming industrial assets. Autoclass is likely to be one of them.

headline: BYD profits collapsed 55% year-on-year in Q1 2026, with Berkshire Hathaway having exited its position entirely in 2025.
reasoning: BYD is China's largest EV maker and was a famous holding of Charlie Munger and Warren Buffett via Berkshire Hathaway. Despite its market-leading position, profits fell 55% year-on-year in Q1 2026, illustrating the severity of margin compression across the Chinese auto sector. Berkshire wisely sold out of the stock entirely in 2025.
quote: The market leader BYD, which was set to be one of Charlie Mongan and Warren Buffett's favorite investments, saw profit decline by 55%. And Berkshire has wisely sold out of the stock entirely in 2025.

headline: Geely profit fell 27% year-on-year in Q1 2026 amid China's brutal auto market conditions.
reasoning: As the number two car maker in China, Geely has not been immune to the sector-wide margin pressure. Q1 2026 results showed profit declining 27% year-on-year, reflecting weak domestic demand and intense price competition from hundreds of new model launches.
quote: So in the first quarter of 2026 results, profit fell by 27% year on year for Gee-lee and 10% for Cherry. And these are the number two and three car makers in China.

headline: Japan's AGC is reducing auto glass capex in absolute terms, signalling a retreat from expansion that benefits Fuyao.
reasoning: AGC was formerly the world leader in auto glass but is now roughly half the size of Fuyao by sales and generates only one-eighth the operating profit with far inferior margins. Its auto glass capex is expected to decrease in absolute terms in the current year, suggesting it is ceding ground to Fuyao rather than competing aggressively. AGC's diversification into construction and industrial materials contrasts with Fuyao's singular focus on auto glass.
quote: A decade ago, when Japan's AGC was the world leader, Fuyao Glass is almost twice AGC size by sales and eight times operating profit and with far superior margin and returns on capital... For AGC, the autoclass capex is also expected to decrease in absolute terms this year.

headline: Lens Technology is an emerging but currently small risk to Fuyao Glass, having begun building auto glass capacity and supplying side windows.
reasoning: Lens Technology is primarily a manufacturer of mobile phone screens and cockpit components but has been building auto glass capacity in recent years and has started supplying side windows to car makers. However, its current scale is described as very small relative to Fuyao, making it a distant rather than immediate competitive threat. Marathon is monitoring the situation given the risk that high returns at Fuyao could attract new entrants.
quote: A Chinese-listed company, Lens Technology, they are a manufacturer of mobile phone screens and cockpit components. They have been building autoclass capacity in the recent years and they are starting to supply side windows. Our research suggests that its scale is currently very small relative to Fuyao, so it remains a distant risk, but it is worth monitoring.

headline: Chinese auto industry facing severe overcapacity and collapsing profits as domestic demand weakens and exports fail to compensate.
reasoning: China's auto factory capacity stands at roughly 55 million units versus domestic sales of only 25 million — enough to supply two-thirds of global demand. Domestic EV demand has weakened after Beijing halved purchase tax exemptions and cut trade-in subsidies, resulting in a 20% year-on-year decline in the first half of 2026. Despite a 50% increase in exports, total EV shipments still fell 4%. The hyper-competitive market has seen some 650 new or refreshed models introduced in the first half alone, squeezing profits industry-wide.
quote: Because there's so much competition, the auto makers are in a race to release new products. About 650 new or refreshed models were introduced in the first half, and that is nearly four per day. This intensive competitive pressure has met with an even weaker demand, leading to lower profits for all the auto manufacturers.

headline: Marathon AM sees Japan corporate buybacks as a multi-year structural opportunity driven by TSE pressure and record cash piles
reasoning: The Tokyo Stock Exchange's 2023 campaign urging companies to address below-book valuations catalysed a two-to-three times increase in buyback plan announcements. Over 50% of TOPIX non-financial companies sit on net cash, and around 35% hold cash above 20% of equity, suggesting the buyback cycle has significant runway. The end of Japan's deflationary era and rising inflation (near 3%) further erode the value of idle cash earning only 0.4%, making buybacks economically compelling. Marathon views this as still in early stages, with the combination of corporate restructuring, balance sheet optimisation, and shareholder-friendly management signalling driving long-term EPS compounding well above headline profit growth.
quote: Japanese companies are doing rather well at the moment as a whole. They're generating cash. And this data that I talk about suggests that over 50% of topics, non-financial, are still sitting on net cash. Around 35% have a substantial amount of net cash, in other words, cash above 20% of their equity. So I think there's plenty more to go for. As I said, when we meet management, we aim to encourage them to think about improving the capital structure of their businesses. So I'm not saying that buybacks are the be all and end all. What we want to see is improvements in earnings power for the corporates that we invest in. But if they can, at the same time, optimize the balance sheets, then that's the icing on the cake.

headline: Marathon holds Kinden, which bought back 17% of shares from Kansai Electric at a discount, boosting EPS ~20% using existing cash
reasoning: Kinden purchased a 17% stake back from former parent Kansai Electric Power for 220 billion yen, funded almost entirely from its existing 200 billion yen cash balance. The transaction enhanced earnings per share by approximately 20% before interest costs, and the company still holds 130 billion yen of cross-shareholdings available for further monetisation. The only caveat is that Kinden missed the opportunity to buy back shares at the maximum 45% discount to book seen in 2023, so book value per share was marginally diluted, though Marathon focuses on intrinsic rather than accounting value.
quote: One of the stocks that we've owned for a while is called Kinden, which is a good case in point. And it recently announced that it was going to buy back 17% of its shares outstanding in one go from Kansai Electric Power, which was many years ago, the original parent company. This cost them 220 billion yen, but it just so happened that they had 200 billion yen sitting there on the balance sheet doing nothing. They also had 130 billion, still do in fact, have 130 billion of cross-share holdings. So the impact on buying back that stock as far as the balance sheet is concerned, it's wholly beneficial. It has the nice effect of enhancing earnings by around 20% before you take interest costs into account.

headline: Marathon holds SECOM as a laggard buyback candidate with 330 billion yen cash pile; models 32% EPS upside if it leverages balance sheet to repurchase stock
reasoning: SECOM dominates Japan's electronic security market with over 40% market share and has converted more than 100% of net income into free cash flow over five years, yet sits on a 330 billion yen cash pile earning a negative real return. The company has begun buying back shares since 2022 but at an insufficient pace to reduce the cash balance meaningfully. Marathon models that SECOM could deploy over 800 billion yen in buybacks, taking net debt to equity to only 33% while boosting EPS by 32%. Activist investor Dalton has filed shareholder resolutions pushing for larger buybacks, and Marathon engages management discretely toward the same end.
quote: One of which is SECOM, which is the number one security company in Japan. So it's got a very large market share in its domestic business. It's got over 40% of the electronic security market. It generates tremendous amounts of cash. So it's converted more than 100% of its net income into free cash flow over the last five years. And it's sitting on a 330 billion yen cash pile, again, not earning a real return. It has brought back some shares starting in 2022, but not enough to keep its cash pile at that very high level... I think that they could spend over 800 billion buying back stock. That would only take their net debt to equity to 33%. And that could boost earnings per share by 32%.

headline: Marathon holds NTT as a 20-year buyback compounder that has grown EPS at 6.5% despite only 2% profit growth by retiring half its share count
reasoning: NTT has repurchased and cancelled roughly half its shares outstanding since 2002, compounding EPS at 6.5% per annum against only 2% annual net profit growth. This has translated into total shareholder returns of approximately 370% over 20 years, well ahead of TOPIX's 270%. The company exemplifies the Buffett thesis that disciplined, below-intrinsic-value repurchases can significantly enhance per-share value even in a low-growth business.
quote: It's not the most exciting company in the world in many ways, but it has been buying back its shares very regularly for the last 20 years to the extent that since I was looking at the numbers since 2002, it's bought back and cancelled roughly half of its shares outstanding. And this has been good for shareholders despite a less than exhilarating pace of profits growth at the firm. So if you look at the 20-year numbers, it's grown its profits at roughly 2% a year, so nothing really to write home about. But if you look at the per share data, so they've been using the cash flows generated to buy back stock regularly, as mentioned, they've managed to compound earnings per share at 6.5%, which is actually well ahead of the 4.5% that you've seen achieved by topics. As a result of that, the shares have performed pretty well. So again, on that 20-year period, they've returned about 370%, and that's against the topics, which has returned about 270%.

headline: Marathon owns Hitachi as a restructuring-plus-buyback compounder with room to accelerate repurchases after balance sheet deleveraging
reasoning: Hitachi transformed from Japan's largest-ever corporate loss in 2009 into a tightly focused industrial company by systematically divesting or IPO-ing non-core units over 15 years. Shares only achieved meaningful re-rating when the company announced a 200 billion yen buyback in 2023, signalling pro-shareholder intent to outside investors. Marathon believes there is scope for substantially more buybacks given the balance sheet has actually been strengthened since 2023, and further repurchases would reinforce management's commitment to capital efficiency.
quote: I think clearly perceptions matter. And the company had been through this extensive process of restructuring for a number of years, but the shares hadn't really done very much relative to the market. But in 2023, they announced a major buyback, 200 billion yen, and that really got the shares moving. They've continued to buy back stock since then, but we think there's space for them to do quite a lot more, in fact, because they've actually delivered the balance sheet in that time since 2023.

headline: Marathon owns Japan Post Holdings, which bought back shares at less than half book value over two years, growing both EPS and book value per share
reasoning: Over the two years to March 2026, Japan Post bought back approximately 600 billion yen of stock at less than half book value, enhancing EPS by around 13% and book value per share by around 10%. Marathon believes reported book value actually understates intrinsic value because the company holds extensive property not marked to fair market value. The combination of a growing book value per share and an undervalued asset base makes Japan Post a particularly compelling buyback candidate.
quote: Japan Post Holdings. This is data from two years running up to March, 2026. It bought back around 600 billion yen of stock at less than half book. And as a result, it enhanced earnings per share by around 13%, but it also enhanced book value per share by around 10%. So you're in this rather enviable position where the more shares you buy back, the cheaper you get. And you actually think in the case of Japan Post, the reported book value is a reasonable proxy for economic value. We actually think that book value understates the real value in this business, largely because they've got extensive property holdings, which are not reflected in the balance sheet at what we think is a fair market value.

headline: Marathon holds Seria, which bought back 17% of shares from its founder at an all-time low price-to-book, lifting EPS by 19%
reasoning: Seria negotiated a buyback of 17% of its shares outstanding from its retiring founder at what the company describes as an all-time low in price-to-book terms. The transaction was funded from cash on hand and resulted in a 19% enhancement of per-share earnings. This is cited as a near-ideal example of the Buffett criterion — buying back stock well below intrinsic value with a strong balance sheet.
quote: This is one another recent one, which is a Japanese discount retailer called Seria, which also by coincidence bought back 17% of its shares outstanding, this time from its founder, who's no longer involved in the business. And they managed to negotiate a brilliant deal where they bought back the stock, effectively an all time low in terms of price to book. And again, they used cash that was already on hand. So buying back 17% of the shares outstanding resulted in a 19% enhancement of per share earnings.

headline: Held as a long-term core position, citing European policy tailwinds and significant earnings upside from closing the North America–Europe margin gap
reasoning: ArcelorMittal is one of the largest global steel producers with ~55 million tonnes of annual output and a vertically integrated model covering ~72% of its iron ore needs internally. Marathon has held the stock through a prolonged period of pressure from Chinese overcapacity, attracted by the Mittal family's 45% stake and aligned capital allocation — notably $11bn spent repurchasing ~38% of shares since 2020, delivering 33% accretion to remaining holders. European operations currently generate far less profit per tonne than North American ones despite producing three times the volume, but 2026 EU policy changes (carbon border adjustment, halving of tariff-free import quotas, and doubling tariffs to 50%) are expected to dramatically close that gap. Titus argues that when policy intervention is mission-critical, sustainable, and rational, it can engineer oligopoly-like conditions and discipline capacity, making it highly lucrative for capital cycle investors.
quote: Yes, Arcelor-Mital's earnings power in Europe can change and expand without any change in Chinese supply thanks to conducive policy. So from a capital cycle perspective, investors need to look at how the state is intervening and changing competitive dynamics industries, not just steel. Interventions in various forms such as tariffs, quotas, carbon borders, security reviews, or sheer political necessities can influence economic profitability that would otherwise prevail in a free market in both directions. When industries are mission critical and interventions sustainable and rational, they can be lucrative for capital cycle investors.

headline: Deglobalisation is rearranging capital cycles: state-directed trade barriers are replacing free-market competition as the force determining industry profitability.
reasoning: Marathon's thesis is that deglobalisation does not abandon the capital cycle framework — high returns attract competition, compress margins, capital exits — but instead substitutes state intervention for free-market forces. Tariffs, quotas, carbon borders, security reviews and political necessity can artificially engineer the supply discipline that excess-capacity industries would otherwise need decades to achieve through market forces alone. Titus argues that in mission-critical industries where interventions are sustainable and rational, these state actions can be highly lucrative for capital cycle investors, effectively converting global commodity markets into domestic oligopolies. Investors must therefore analyse not just competitive dynamics and supply/demand, but also the trajectory of government policy.
quote: Yes, the orthodox capital cycle dynamic of high returns, inviting competition, returns compressing, capital exiting and so on isn't actually abandoned. It's rearranged by the state instead of free market forces... We see a retreat from the doctrine of free trade and comparative advantage. This has altered capital cycles of the US and European steel industries in place of global competition and excess supply. These regions now resemble oligopolies with disciplined Kappa City control. Which at least from a capital cycle perspective should be good news for investors in those sectors.

headline: US steel industry transformed into a high-margin oligopoly by Section 232 tariffs, with ArcelorMittal North America generating $180/tonne operating profit — well above historical range.
reasoning: The first Trump administration introduced Section 232 national-security tariffs on steel imports in 2018, citing the strategic importance of domestic steel for defence and infrastructure. This framework has enjoyed bipartisan support across subsequent administrations. The tariffs increased domestic utilisation rates and lifted US steel prices, enabling ArcelorMittal's North American segment to generate $180 of operating profit per tonne since then, above both its historical range and the group average. Titus uses this as a template for what European policy could achieve if the 2026 measures prove similarly effective.
quote: Yes, the fortune for acylar metal in North America changed in 2018. Washington viewed imported steel as an issue of national security. A weak domestic steel industry was viewed as a strategic weakness because steel plays a key role in the making of ships, tanks, aircrafts, missiles, rails, grids, pipelines, you name it. And so what did the Trump administration do? To keep the domestic steel industry afloat, the US needed higher utilization rates. Best way to do that was to increase domestic prices, which they did by introducing tariffs under the section 232. The framework has survived presidents from both sides of the aisle, indicating p-partisan support. As a result, Arcelor Metal's North American segment generated $180 of operating profit per ton since then, ahead of its historical range and group average.

headline: European steel sector set to benefit from 2026 EU policy reset — halved import quotas and doubled tariffs expected to restore domestic profitability.
reasoning: The EU's initial 2019 tariff-and-quota regime backfired because quotas were pegged to rising prior import volumes while actual demand was falling, allowing more Chinese steel into the market than before. From mid-2026, the EU is cutting tariff-free import quotas by half to 18 million tonnes and doubling the out-of-quota tariff rate from 25% to 50%, which should reduce the import share to ~15% of the market. In addition, the carbon border adjustment introduced at the start of 2026 levels the playing field between European producers — who must buy carbon credits or reduce emissions — and Chinese blast-furnace producers with far higher greenhouse emissions. Titus frames these as structural changes that effectively convert the European steel market from a dumping ground into a disciplined oligopoly, materially improving the earnings power of incumbents like ArcelorMittal.
quote: From 1st of July, tariff free import quotas will be cut in half to 18 million tons, while the tariff rate will double from 25% to 50%. This should reduce the share of imports to 15%... For example, in 2024, Arcelor-Meta produced three times more steel in Europe than in North America, yet its North American segment generated more profits for the company. If that gap in cash margin per ton between those two regions can close, the upside is enormous.

headline: thyssenkrupp announced 11,000 job cuts amid European steel industry pain caused by failed EU import quota design and Chinese overcapacity.
reasoning: Titus cites thyssenkrupp's 11,000 job cuts as evidence of the severity of damage wrought on the European steel sector by the failure of the EU's 2019 quota regime. The policy allowed growing volumes of tariff-free Chinese imports at a time when European demand was falling, squeezing domestic producers. ArcelorMittal also idled parts of its capacity during this period. The mention is illustrative of industry stress rather than a direct investment view on thyssenkrupp itself.
quote: Pain. Arcelor Metal idled parts of its capacity. Tissen Group, another European steelmaker, announced 11,000 drop cuts. Import competition became a luxury Europe could not longer afford. It forced European lawmakers to revisit their approach.

headline: China's steel overcapacity and subsidised exports have structurally impaired Western steel industry economics since 2008, with no near-term resolution visible.
reasoning: China's rapid industrialisation in the early 2000s drove a commodity supercycle that benefited global steel producers enormously. However, China simultaneously built out enormous domestic steelmaking capacity while the 2008 GFC vaporised demand, creating structural oversupply — global excess capacity reached over 700 million tonnes, meaning 40% more steel was produced than consumed. The subsequent decline in China's property market from 2014 made things worse. Western markets became dumping grounds for subsidised Chinese exports. Titus notes that China's steel is predominantly produced via coal-fired blast furnaces with far higher emissions than European electric arc furnaces, which is now relevant to the carbon border adjustment regime.
quote: It peaked with China consuming as much steel as the rest of the world combined. And then 2008 global financial crisis came, vaporized demand, while China has been building out enormous domestic capacity in parallel. This created structural oversupply, which only got worse as Chinese property market, another big demand source, entered a downtrend in 2014... Back then, global capacity reached the excess of 700 million tons. In other words, we are producing 40% more than we consumed, and the western markets became the dumping ground for the excess supply from China.

headline: Marathon owns Invista Holdings, a dental manufacturer, as a capital cycle play overlooked by passive and retail investors
reasoning: Invista Holdings is described as a dental manufacturer offering a compelling capital cycle investment thesis. Like TransUnion, it has been left behind by the AI-driven market rally and trades at valuations not seen for years relative to an expensive broader market. Its lack of fit with the AI/semiconductor narrative has created a valuation opportunity for active stock-pickers.
quote: At Marathon, we've got exposure to smaller companies like TransUnion, a credit bureau or Invista Holdings, a dental manufacturer, both offering a compelling capital cycle investment thesis. And even our larger holdings, things like Visa, offer high quality business models at very attractive valuations, the opportunity presenting itself because these companies don't fit the market's prevailing narrative.

headline: NASDAQ 100 fast-track inclusion — with rules changed to remove free float minimums and grant 3x free float weighting — risks amplifying passive price distortion
reasoning: SpaceX sought fast-track inclusion in both the S&P 500 and NASDAQ 100, gaming index rules to capture passive buying flows. NASDAQ capitulated, adjusting rules to allow SpaceX entry in just 15 trading days and removing the minimum free float requirement, granting SpaceX a weighting of three times its free float. Warrum notes that even though a free float multiple is better than full market cap weighting, the 3x multiplier will amplify index purchases and drive the price higher. He draws a historical parallel with Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom in the late 1990s, where over-weighting relative to free float created squeezes in those stocks.
quote: NASDAQ adjusted its rules to allow SpaceX to enter the NASDAQ 100 index in just 15 trading days. And then they also removed the minimum free float requirement. They're going to give SpaceX a weighting of three times the free float in the index. Now, admittedly, this is better than market cap weighting approach. But even so, three times will amplify the index purchases and drive the price up further. This question of over-weighting a stock relative to its free float in an index — with some people with long memories or long experience — will remember that this was exactly the problems that the MSCI indices had at the turn of the century.

headline: Top nine companies in MSCI US and S&P 500 all design semiconductors, representing 37% of the index — concentration typical of late-stage bubble markets

headline: Passive inflows create a self-reinforcing liquidity loop that inflates mega-cap valuations, particularly those tied to the AI theme
reasoning: Tom Warrum argues that the largest index constituents have lower liquidity per dollar of free float than smaller constituents, meaning passive inflows have a disproportionately larger price impact on the largest stocks. As inflows push up mega-cap prices, indices must buy more of those risen stocks, further reducing their effective free float and cementing the liquidity imbalance. This self-reinforcing loop has driven concentration in the S&P 500 and MSCI US Index around a single AI-semiconductor theme, with the top nine companies in each index all involved in semiconductor design comprising 37% of the index. Warrum contends this dynamic means passive investing is no longer truly passive — indices are effectively portfolios with weights determined by flows and liquidity rather than fundamental analysis.
quote: If we look at the 20 companies with the largest weights in the MSCI US Index, 16 of them, so 80%, have liquidity as a percentage of free float that is lower than the index average. So if we put this a different way, if you wanted to trade a large inflow into this index, it's going to take longer to trade the largest positions than the smallest positions. So the price impact of that inflow is going to be greater on the largest index constituents. And also that works in reverse. So it's the same for the outflows. They will have a greater price impact on the largest constituents.

headline: Memory chip oligopoly facing Chinese disruption as CXMT scales DRAM capacity, threatening to erode supernormal margins

headline: Warns AI capex cycle is crowding out real economy investment and poses systemic risk to equity markets

quote: And some of the areas where you're putting your money is actually in the bubble areas of yesteryear, namely Chinese real estate. Yeah, I think that Chinese real estate is an area where we've seen a huge contraction of activity... There are other markets that have been totally neglected.

headline: Samsung Electronics cited as a bellwether of EM AI trade with gross margins having run from 15% to 90%, making further extrapolation unrealistic
reasoning: Samsung was one of the initial bellwethers of the AI picks-and-shovels trade in EM. Operating margins have expanded dramatically, with gross margins in some instances running from 15% to 90%, reflecting the current tight supply-demand environment. Duffy argues this level of profitability cannot be extrapolated and that valuation risk has become the dominant concern. New memory supply is coming on in late 2027/early 2028, which will turn the capital cycle.
quote: I think that right now, there is clearly a very tight supply demand picture. And so that's an interesting point in the capital cycle, but that's priced by the fact that operating margins in the case of Samsung Electronics have gone from 15% to 90% gross margins in some instances. We wouldn't say that you can extrapolate that for any extent of time.

headline: Held as a genuine technological moat but now more cautious on valuation risk relative to business quality
reasoning: TSMC has been a portfolio holding for five to seven years and beyond, with management regarded as good stewards of capital. Duffy acknowledges TSMC dominates its end-profit pool through a technological moat, distinguishing it from more commoditized supply chain participants. However, at this stage of the cycle, valuation risk is overawing business risk even for high-quality names. The research focus has shifted toward understanding the degree to which current profitability levels are being extrapolated into the future over an unrealistically long timeframe.
quote: We've had significant exposure to some of these businesses, Taiwan Semi, Delta Electronics, Media Tech. They've comprised the portfolio over the last five to seven years and beyond in the case of TSMC. Management teams have been good stewards of capital. That said, we are at the stage of the cycle where the business risk, which is predominantly what the management teams would be able to control and to focus on, is being overawed by the valuation risk and the crowd-like behavior of markets.

headline: Korea and Taiwan now represent ~45% of MSCI EM, up from ~25%, creating dangerous concentration risk in emerging market portfolios
reasoning: The AI thematic has shifted focus from US hyperscalers to the picks-and-shovels tech supply chain, predominantly in Korea and Taiwan. Their combined weight in MSCI EM has jumped from around 25% to 45% in just over a year, a 20-point move that is historically unprecedented for that index. Semiconductors, tech hardware, and equipment now represent approximately 38% of EM, up from 18-20% eighteen months ago. This concentration means global portfolios are increasingly correlated to a single trade, and asset allocators need to be mindful of their true exposure when constructing diversified equity portfolios.
quote: So the focus of the AI thematic has really, in the last 12 months, moved away from the US hyperscalers towards the picks and shovels, so the tech supply chain, predominantly in Korea and Taiwan, Samsung Electronics, TSMC, were the bellwethers initially, but it's gone far deeper than that into some more esoteric companies that comprise those indexes. So they now stand at 45% or so of MSCI emerging markets... And that is up from 25%, and in other words, a 20-point move in the course of a little more than a year, which is a remarkable move.

headline: Trading at 9x earnings after 7-8x earnings growth but cyclicality risk is being ignored by simple PE analysis
reasoning: Edward Chancellor notes that Micron is trading at approximately nine times earnings, but those earnings are up seven to eightfold in the last year, making the PE ratio an unreliable guide to valuation. The host and Duffy agree that using PE multiples for highly cyclical businesses at peak earnings significantly understates valuation risk. New memory supply coming on in late 2027 and early 2028 will likely reverse the current tight supply-demand dynamic.
quote: I don't know about your emerging names, but I see the Micron Technology is trading on nine times earnings. Now, those earnings are up seven or eightfold in the last year. But tell me what you see as the valuation risk for these businesses.

headline: Marathon AM reducing EM tech supply chain exposure as price-to-book multiples have inflated 4-6x, creating a 'fundamental bubble' even if PE looks optically cheap
reasoning: Duffy argues that the EM tech supply chain trades at superficially attractive PE multiples of around 20x earnings, but this misses the fact that price-to-book multiples have inflated four to five to six fold. He characterises this as a 'fundamental bubble' or 'earnings bubble' where current peak margins are being capitalised into valuations, drawing a direct parallel to the mining super cycle where miners traded at 10x earnings but at inflated EV/invested capital multiples. The deep commodity component suppliers have seen the most hyperbolic share price moves and are explicitly described as 'time and capital businesses' where capital is now abundant. The analogy is that the tech supply chain re-rating is a response to a false price signal from over-investment on uneconomic projects inside the US.
quote: Today, the tech supply chain, you'll hear quotes such as that it's attractively valued on 20 times earnings, but that ignores the fact that the price to book multiples have gone up by four, five, six fold. And so it's an earnings bubble. It's not a valuation bubble. Because that's what I call a fundamental bubble. When the bubble is in the balance sheet or in the earnings, I call that a fundamental bubble. And most investors or people who think about markets always look at just simple valuation metrics on the PE basis and say, look, microns on nine times earnings is cheap. Which misses the cyclicality of the business.

headline: Marathon AM holds Auto Trader, viewing its vertical automotive data and dealer workflow tools as defensible against horizontal AI competitors
reasoning: Carter argues Auto Trader's leading position in the UK used-car market is underpinned by deep proprietary data on vehicle history, specification and provenance that is difficult for horizontal AI to replicate. Beyond the consumer-facing portal, Auto Trader provides significant value to car dealer customers through workflow management, inventory tools and AI-enhanced productivity features. He believes the company can leverage these AI capabilities offensively to defend its vertical moat.
quote: So for a real estate agent, if they know that Eddie Chancellor is looking at a new country property, they can identify that he may be looking to sell his existing property that's a lead that they can pass on and sell effectively to an estate agent. So there's value in the system from what they do. And similarly, for something like an auto trader, they are doing a lot of work helping with the workflow and inventory management and various other things to help their car dealers become more productive. And of course, they can use AI tools. It's the chief executive of Reitmütze. It's not rocket science. They can use a lot of these AI tools to add to their vertical expertise, to fend off the competition from the more horizontally oriented AI companies.

headline: Marathon AM warns AI-driven sector rotation mirrors TMT bubble dynamics, with markets prematurely writing off old-economy businesses
reasoning: Charles Carter argues that current financial markets are highly speculative, with capital crowding into technology stocks and leaving other sectors for dead — a pattern closely resembling the TMT boom of the late 1990s. He cites Economist research showing the market correctly identifies secular losers only about half the time, barely better than a coin toss. He believes some AI-disruptee stocks have been oversold and may recover strongly, particularly those with proprietary data assets and adaptable management teams. He cautions investors who wait for a clear catalyst will likely miss the rally when it comes.
quote: There's a chance, I believe, that there are companies now which have been beaten up for reasons to do with AI, which may indeed recover strongly because they have assets and management teams that can adapt to the new scenario. The game, if you like, of spot the winners and losers was a very popular one in that period you mentioned that the TMT boom of the late 1990s when the new economy winners were sort of lauded over the old economy losers.

headline: Marathon AM holds RELX, arguing its proprietary legal, scientific and risk data becomes more valuable rather than less in the AI era
reasoning: Carter describes RELX as a must-have information company with a highly valuable and hard-to-replicate proprietary dataset spanning legal case law (LexisNexis), scientific journals (Elsevier), and auto insurance risk data. He notes that AI tools like Protégé added to the LexisNexis database have actually increased usage and enabled pricing increases, growing revenues and profits. He contrasts RELX's deterministic, curated approach to data with the probabilistic, hallucination-prone nature of LLMs, arguing the core data business remains defensible. The risk of new entrants like Harvey and Claude is acknowledged but viewed as a threat to analytics rather than to the underlying data asset.
quote: You've seen that a little bit so far with Rellex's legal business, where it has been adding AI tools such as Protégé to the Lexus Nexus database, and that's been enabling them to see greater usage of the database, and that allows them to increase pricing. So actually, the revenues and profits in that area have actually been increasing in the age of AI so far. The question I think a lot of people will have is whether or not the advent of a lot of new entrants into this field, such as Harvey, Ligora, and latterly with Claude making a big push in this area, how that's going to create more competition in the sort of analytics side of the business. But I believe that the core data business is very hard to replicate.

headline: Marathon AM has exited staffing and recruitment positions on the view that AI poses an existential threat to the sector
reasoning: Carter states Marathon has taken a hard look at AI's impact across the portfolio and concluded that staffing and recruitment businesses are genuinely at risk, leading to full exits from positions in that sector. This represents a deliberate portfolio decision based on the view that AI will displace substantial demand for recruitment and staffing services. He contrasts this with his more optimistic view on proprietary data and online classified businesses.
quote: We've had companies in the portfolio where we've taken a good hard look at the impact of AI and decided that they are at risk. So we've exited a number of positions in the field of staffing and recruitment as a result of that, as well as certain media assets that look vulnerable in the age of AI.

headline: Booking Holdings cited as an example of a vertical marketplace where deep supplier relationships make AI disintermediation very difficult
reasoning: Carter references a third-party view (from investor Johnson Tepper) on Booking Holdings as supporting evidence for his thesis that vertical marketplace businesses with deep, proprietary supplier relationships are hard to disintermediate. He notes that OpenAI itself has reportedly stopped trying to compete with Booking Holdings and is now sending it traffic — a real-world data point that horizontal AI cannot easily replicate the depth of relationships in established vertical platforms.
quote: I have a friend, Johnson Tepper, who wrote about a stock in Bookings Holdings, which owns a number of travel websites. And he said that they have so many relationships with so many different hotels and other holiday businesses that there is no way that the likes of OpenAI can actually get into their business. And OpenAI has actually stopped trying to do that as it is now sending them traffic.

headline: Marathon AM has limited exposure to SAP and views the jury as still out on whether it can leverage its data assets to win in the AI era
reasoning: Carter notes SAP is the dominant European software business facing AI disruption questions but that Marathon has had little exposure to the SaaS/enterprise software theme in Europe. He frames SAP as a live debate — the company has valuable corporate data as a system of record, but it is unclear whether management can translate that into AI-era competitive advantage. He does not express a clear positive or negative view, treating it as an open question.
quote: The big company in Europe is SAP, which has been suffering and the jury is still out as to whether or not they can really leverage their assets in terms of the data that they have on companies and their position as a system of record in the corporate ecosystem, whether they can leverage that to actually be a winner in the AI world. So there's a big debate about that.

headline: Marathon AM holds Rightmove, arguing its domain expertise and three-sided marketplace moat can withstand AI disintermediation risk
reasoning: Carter acknowledges the bear case — that agentic AI could bypass vertical property portals like Rightmove entirely, scraping listings and disintermediating the network effect. However, he argues that Rightmove possesses deep proprietary data and domain expertise that large horizontal AI models lack, including granular property history and buyer behaviour data that is hard to replicate. He also highlights the value Rightmove provides to estate agent customers via lead generation and workflow tools. He believes Rightmove can use AI tools offensively to defend and extend its moat against horizontal AI competitors.
quote: There's a lot of data in both of these examples of the verticals, both houses and in cars, where there's more proprietary data than meets the eye, details about the car's history, its exact specification. It's much harder to scrape all of that information as opposed to knowing the specific identifying number of the car and then all the history of the car crashes and so forth. So they can build up a lot of expertise around both houses and cars. And then of course, there's the other side of what they do, which is the value that they bring to their real estate agent and car dealer customers.

headline: Marathon AM holds Experian, viewing its contributory credit data as largely AI-proof given its non-public, numerical and machine-to-machine nature
reasoning: Carter argues Experian's credit bureau data is contributed voluntarily by banks and other financial institutions, meaning it is not available on the public internet and cannot be scraped by AI models. The data is also numerical and transmitted machine-to-machine, insulating it from the per-seat model disruption that threatens some software businesses. He draws a historical parallel to GUS (Great Universal Stores), which owned the precursor credit business and was a beaten-down old-economy stock that rebounded strongly after the dot-com crash. He views Experian as having a similarly durable moat in the AI era.
quote: There, I think the data, as I say, is contributing data so it's not actually available on the internet. So it's much harder to replicate. To scrape and steal. To scrape and steal. And it's also numerical. I mean, LLMs are very good at language, obviously, and may, of course, get much better when it comes to data. But it is numerical data and it tends to be passed through to the consumer on a kind of machine-to-machine basis. So you don't have this risk that you have fewer analysts working at customers who may be losing their jobs and the old per-seat model that you have, in some cases, in the services industry is undermined.
